description: simulaciones de sonidos de los astros
summary: An application was developed that converts images and information about the Earth into a multisensory experience. It uses real-time data such as weather, temperature, and wind speed to find the location of the image, assigns frequencies to these parameters, and maps them to musical scales to generate real songs. This offers an accessible and simple way for visually impaired people to listen to the Earth.
details:
An application was developed that converts NASA scientific data into real soundscapes and music, turning geospatial and climate information into a sensory experience. It takes a location entered by the user and calculates its spatial boundaries (bounding box) through geolocation. It then automatically downloads satellite atmospheric data files (MERRA-2) in NetCDF-4 format (.nc4) through NASA’s API, and processes and filters them, tabulating the data into CSV files.

The musical logic works on two levels. First, it uses the absolute latitude and the distance to the Earth’s imaginary lines to determine the organological and instrumental identity of the region: the intertropical band is assigned percussion and the pentatonic scale, temperate zones are assigned chordophones and the Dorian mode, and polar zones are assigned aerophones and the Phrygian mode. Second, dynamic variables such as wind speed and pressure are used to modulate frequencies across 12 semitones and multiple octaves, which breaks linearity and generates polyphony and variable chords in real time.

The application was developed in Python, using scientific and data libraries: earthaccess to connect with NASA’s databases, xarray and pandas to handle NetCDF-4 arrays and tabular processing, numpy and scipy for mathematical calculation and audio synthesis (.wav), and geopy for geolocation. It is deployed and accessible on the web through the Render platform.

This offers an innovative and intuitive way to democratize and communicate climate science, turning abstract data into an artistic, sensory experience. It is expected to serve as a tool for science outreach and environmental education in museums, institutions, and academic settings, fostering interest in space science and geography through auditory art.

Its creativity lies in the interdisciplinary fusion of satellite astrophysics/climatology and cultural anthropology (organology). Instead of plotting a conventional visual map, it gives the planet a “voice” of its own, where geography defines the cultural instrument and the atmosphere composes the harmony.

The team prioritized technical robustness in the bulk download of satellite data, theoretical independence (instrument assignment is separated strictly from astronomical latitude to avoid biases caused by local thermal anomalies), and precision in frequency quantization through modal scales and octaves, so that the final result would be musically harmonious and aesthetically pleasing.
